query: For an FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating susceptible to progressive plastic deformation during continuous loading, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its creep resistance? Specify the governing factor and rationale, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, the operating boundaries under sustained stress, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Tuning the alloy composition to induce a moderate negative γ/γ′ lattice misfit in the FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy coating increases interfacial coherency, thereby impeding dislocation transmission and improving creep resistance under continuous loading.
generation.material_initial_state: FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy protective coating fabricated with a conventional composition exhibiting near-zero or slightly positive γ/γ′ lattice misfit.
generation.intervention: Adjust the alloy composition to achieve a moderate negative γ/γ′ lattice misfit.
generation.conditions: Sustained high-stress (around 2.0–3.0 GPa) and elevated temperature (approximately 1000 K) conditions representative of service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced coherency and strengthened γ/γ′ interfaces acting as effective barriers to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: The moderate negative lattice misfit improves the coherency of the γ/γ′ interfaces, which impedes the transmission and accumulation of dislocations across the interface. This results in delayed dislocation nucleation and slower progressive plastic deformation (creep) under sustained loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: When compared to the baseline, the composition-tuned alloy will exhibit lower creep strain rates, reduced dislocation activity at the γ/γ′ interfaces, and overall enhanced creep resistance.
generation.baseline: The standard FCC/BCC HESA with conventional composition showing higher creep strain and dislocation transmission under similar sustained loading conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions where the moderate negative misfit enhances interfacial strength; if the misfit is too large (excessive interfacial strain) or not adequately induced, the beneficial effect on creep resistance may be lost.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal range of the negative misfit and the quantitative improvement in creep rate require further experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy coatings: a baseline group with the conventional composition and an experimental group with the composition modified to induce a moderate negative γ/γ′ lattice misfit. Subject both groups to sustained loading at 2.0–3.0 GPa and constant temperature near 1000 K. Use in situ creep testing combined with transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to monitor dislocation motion and interface structure.
measurements: Dislocation density and distribution via TEM
Quantitative measurements of γ/γ′ lattice misfit (e.g., using XRD or high-resolution TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the composition-tuned samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in creep strain rate and dislocation transmission, or if microstructural analyses do not reveal enhanced interfacial coherency compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: A clear transition in creep mechanisms is observed, evolving from diffusion-dominated deformation at low stresses to dislocation nucleation, glide, and interaction at intermediate conditions, and ultimately to stress-induced phase transformation at higher stresses and temperatures. This progression is corroborated by atomic-scale structural evolution and steady-state creep theory. Under identical conditions, HESAs show markedly superior creep resistance to HEAs, mainly due to the strong blocking effect of γ/γ′ interfaces on dislocation motion and atomic transport. Both the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction exert a critical influence on creep resistance. The relationship between misfit magnitude and creep behavior is non-monotonic: moderate negative misfit enhances interfacial coherency and stabilizes the microstructure, thereby improving creep resistance, whereas excessively large misfit increases interfacial strain energy and deteriorates performance. A negative misfit is generally more effective in resisting creep because it strengthens the γ/γ′ interface and reduces dislocation transmissibility. In addition, increasing the γ′ volume fraction significantly enhances creep

reading.lever: Tune alloy composition to induce a moderate negative γ/γ′ lattice misfit that impedes dislocation transmission.
reading.why: This approach, proven in HESA systems, directly targets the creep mechanism by strengthening interfaces against progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC coatings.
